0.title: Strength and Dignity in Christ
0.overview:
What does it mean to be a woman? Our culture gives many answers, and most of them are exhausting. Some say a woman's worth lies in her beauty, her body and her appeal to others. Some say it lies in her career and independence, and that motherhood or marriage hold her back. Others say womanhood is simply whatever an individual chooses it to be. And sadly, some religious cultures have reduced women to silence and household duties alone, ignoring the many women Scripture honors for their wisdom, courage, faith and work.

The Bible offers something far better. A woman is not defined by her looks, her relationships, her achievements or anyone else's opinion. She is defined by the God who made her. So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them (Gen 1:27). A woman is fully an image-bearer of God, equal in dignity with man, loved by God and called by him.

And the Bible shows us women who lived that calling. Sarah, who hoped in God. Ruth, whose loyal love brought her into the family line of Christ. Hannah, who poured out her heart in prayer. Abigail, whose wisdom stopped a massacre. Mary, who said, Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word (Luke 1:38). The women who stayed at the cross when most of the disciples had fled, and who were the first to hear the news that Jesus had risen. Priscilla, Phoebe, Lydia, Lois and Eunice. Scripture's picture of womanhood is rich, strong and beautiful.

Proverbs gives a summary worth carrying through these studies: Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come (Prov 31:25). Biblical womanhood is a woman's glad embrace of God's design, clothed in strength and dignity, fearing the LORD, and using her gifts to help, nurture and build up others for the glory of Christ.

These studies follow the historic Reformed understanding usually called complementarian: men and women are equal in worth, but God has given them distinct and complementary callings, especially in marriage and in the leadership of the church. Many sincere Christians, usually called egalitarians, read some of the key passages differently, and where those questions arise, their view is explained fairly. These studies are also for every woman: single or married, with children or without, young or old. A woman's calling is not on hold until she marries, and her worth does not depend on whether she becomes a mother.

Above all, womanhood, like manhood, is not a standard to earn God's love. It flows from grace. Every woman who belongs to Christ is part of the bride he loved and gave himself for, and he will present her in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27).

Six units: (1) Made in God's Image: A Helper Fit for Him; (2) Eve, the Fall and the Promised Offspring; (3) Jesus and the Women Who Followed Him; (4) Wives: Strength Under Christ; (5) Women in the Church: Gifts, Ministry and Order; (6) Beauty That Lasts.

1.title: Made in God's Image: A Helper Fit for Him
1.overview:
Womanhood begins in the heart of God. When God created humanity, he made both man and woman in his image (Gen 1:27). Both were blessed. Both were given dominion over the earth. Both were called very good. A woman does not borrow her dignity from a man. She receives it directly from God.

Genesis 2 tells the story in more detail. God formed the man and placed him in the garden. Then God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him (Gen 2:18). The ESV notes that fit for may be translated "corresponding to". The woman would be like the man and yet different from him, his counterpart, the one who completes the picture.

God then made the woman in a remarkable way. The rib he had taken from the man he made into a woman (Gen 2:22). The ESV notes that the Hebrew says God "built" her. She was not made from the dust like the man, but carefully built, as an architect crafts a masterpiece. When Adam saw her, he said, This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man (Gen 2:23). The ESV notes that the Hebrew words for woman and man sound alike. She shared his very nature.

Some people hear the word helper and think it means a servant or an assistant. But the Bible uses the same idea of God himself: Behold, God is my helper (Ps 54:4), and My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth (Ps 121:2). To help is not to be inferior. It is to bring strength that another person needs. The woman's calling as helper is a calling of honor.
1.theology:
Equal image-bearers: Women and men are equally made in God's image, equally fallen and equally redeemed. Peter tells husbands that their wives are heirs with you of the grace of life (1 Pet 3:7). Paul says that in Christ there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal 3:28). No woman is a second-class Christian.

Different and complementary: God did not make two identical people. He made a man and a woman who correspond to each other. Their differences are not flaws to be erased but gifts that allow them to serve together in ways neither could alone. Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman (1 Cor 11:11).

Helper as honor: The woman's calling to help is part of God's good design before the fall, not a punishment after it. Help in the Bible is strength brought alongside another. A godly woman uses her gifts, wisdom and strength to strengthen others, beginning in marriage for those who are married, and extending to her family, church and world.
1.examples:
Worth in a comparison culture: Many women today measure themselves constantly against images of beauty, success and motherhood on their screens, and always come up short. Genesis 1 and 2 speak a better word. Your worth was settled when God made you in his image and built you with care. It is not measured by likes, weight, income or anyone's approval.

Helping without disappearing: Some women hear "helper" and assume they must suppress their gifts, opinions and strength. But the God who is our helper is never weak or silent. A wife who helps her husband brings her whole self: her insight, her counsel, her courage and her faith. Abigail's wisdom later in Scripture shows how valuable a woman's discernment can be.

verseByVerse.quote: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The first description of humanity in the Bible includes women from the very beginning: male and female he created them. The woman is not an afterthought or a lesser copy of the man. She bears the image of God fully. To bear God's image is to reflect his character and to represent his rule in the world. Every woman, whatever her age, ability, marital status or background, carries that dignity. This is the foundation of everything else Scripture says about women.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the first thing in creation God calls not good. The man alone was incomplete. God's answer was to make a helper fit for him, one who corresponds to him. The woman was not created because the man was superior, but because he was lacking. She brought what he needed. In marriage, a wife is her husband's partner in life and in God's calling, his closest ally. Even for a woman who is not married, this verse reminds us that God made human beings for relationship, and that women have a vital role in building up others.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, God is my helper; the Lord is the upholder of my life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David wrote this psalm when he was being hunted by enemies. In his danger he said, Behold, God is my helper. God is not a helper because he is weaker than David. He is a helper because he brings the strength David does not have. This verse transforms how we read Genesis 2:18. When God calls the woman a helper, he is using a word that describes his own care for his people. To help is to be like God.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter calls the wife the weaker vessel, most likely referring to physical strength, not to her mind, spirit or worth. And the very reason he gives for honoring her is that they are heirs with you of the grace of life. A Christian wife is her husband's equal heir of eternal life. Peter adds a warning: a husband who dishonors his wife will find that his prayers are hindered. God takes the dignity of women so seriously that how a man treats his wife affects his relationship with God.

1.reflection:
What messages about womanhood have shaped you most, from family, church or culture? Which of them fit the Bible?

How does it change your view of the word "helper" to know that God calls himself his people's helper?

Genesis says God "built" the woman. How does knowing that you were carefully made by God affect the way you see yourself?

Where are you tempted to find your worth in comparison with other women? What truth from this unit speaks to that?

2.title: Eve, the Fall and the Promised Offspring
2.overview:
The goodness of creation did not last. The serpent came to the woman and questioned God's word: Did God actually say...? Eve listened, doubted God's goodness, and when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate (Gen 3:6).

The New Testament says that the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning (2 Cor 11:3). She was deceived, and Adam, standing beside her, sinned knowingly. Both were guilty. Both hid from God. And both received the consequences. For the woman, the consequences touched the two areas of her life that were meant to bring the greatest joy: childbearing and marriage. I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you (Gen 3:16).

But before God spoke those words to the woman, he spoke a promise to the serpent: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel (Gen 3:15). A child would be born from the woman who would crush the serpent. This is often called the first announcement of the gospel. The ESV notes that offspring is literally "seed", a word that will follow the promise through the whole book of Genesis.

In spite of her sin, Eve was not abandoned. Adam named her Eve, because she was the mother of all living (Gen 3:20), and the ESV notes that her name sounds like the Hebrew for "life-giver". Through the line of women that followed her came, at last, the promised child: when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman (Gal 4:4). The woman through whom sin entered the world was also the woman through whom the Savior was promised.
2.theology:
Deceived but not discarded: Eve's sin was real, and Paul later refers to her deception (1 Tim 2:14; 2 Cor 11:3). But Scripture never treats women as more sinful than men. It was through one man that sin came into the world (Rom 5:12). And God pursued Eve with grace, clothing her and Adam and promising a Savior through her offspring.

The battle between the sexes: The ESV notes that Your desire shall be for your husband may be read "against" your husband, and points to Genesis 4:7, where sin's desire is for you, and you must rule over it. Many understand Genesis 3:16 to describe a struggle that sin brought into marriage: the wife tempted to resist or control her husband, and the husband tempted to dominate her harshly. This conflict is the curse, not God's design. In Christ, husbands and wives are set free to love and serve one another again.

The promised offspring: The whole story of the Bible follows the promise of Genesis 3:15 through the births of children to women like Sarah, Rebekah, Leah, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and finally Mary. God used women again and again to carry forward his plan of salvation.

A hard verse: 1 Timothy 2:15 says that she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control. Christians have understood this in several ways: that women are saved through the birth of the Child, Christ; that women are kept safe through the dangers of childbirth; or that women work out their salvation in faithfully living their God-given calling, including motherhood. Whatever the exact sense, Paul is not teaching that women earn salvation by having babies. Salvation is by grace through faith, for women and men alike.
2.examples:
The lie in the garden today: The serpent's first words were a question about God's goodness: did God really say that? The same lie comes to women today: God's design is restrictive, his commands keep you from happiness, you can be wise without him. Every generation of women, and men, must decide whom to believe.

Pain and promise in motherhood: Many women know the reality of Genesis 3:16 firsthand: the pain of childbirth, miscarriage, infertility, or the heartbreak of raising children in a fallen world. Genesis does not hide that pain. But it also sets it next to a promise. Through a woman's child, God would bring salvation. Every Christian mother raising children in hope, and every woman grieving the children she longed for, can look to the Child who was born to crush the serpent and wipe away every tear.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Eve's sin followed a pattern that is still familiar. She saw that the fruit was good for food and a delight to the eyes. She believed it would make her wise. What God had forbidden began to look desirable, beautiful and smart. Temptation always works this way: it makes disobedience look good. And notice that her sin did not stay with her. She also gave some to her husband. Our sins always affect the people closest to us, just as our faithfulness can bless them.

verseByVerse.quote: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is spoken to the serpent, and it is full of hope for the woman. God himself will put enmity between the woman and the serpent. Eve had listened to the serpent as a friend. God would make them enemies again. And a descendant of the woman would strike the decisive blow: he shall bruise your head, while the serpent would only bruise his heel. That was fulfilled at the cross, where Jesus was wounded and yet defeated Satan. The first gospel promise in the Bible centers on a woman and her child.

verseByVerse.quote: To the woman he said, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God speaks to the woman about two areas of life: childbirth and marriage. Both were meant for joy, and both would now include pain and struggle. The ESV notes that desire may be "against" her husband, like sin's desire in Genesis 4:7. The marriage relationship would become a battleground, with the wife tempted to resist and the husband tempted to rule harshly. This is a description of what sin does, not a command to follow. Christian marriage, shaped by the gospel, is meant to undo this curse, as husbands love sacrificially and wives respond with trust and respect.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul sums up the whole story of redemption in a few words: God sent forth his Son, born of woman. The promise of Genesis 3:15 came true through a woman, Mary. The eternal Son of God entered the world the way every human being does, through a mother's body. God honored womanhood by choosing it as the doorway through which the Savior would come. The woman who first listened to the serpent was the ancestor of the child who would destroy it.

2.reflection:
The serpent began by questioning God's word and goodness. In what ways are women today tempted to doubt that God's design is good?

How does Genesis 3:16 help explain conflict in marriage? How does the gospel offer a way out of that pattern?

Why is it significant that the first promise of a Savior centers on the woman and her offspring?

How might Galatians 4:4, "born of woman", encourage a woman who struggles to see her life as significant?

3.title: Jesus and the Women Who Followed Him
3.overview:
In the world of the first century, women were often overlooked. Many teachers would not teach them, their testimony was often discounted, and even Jesus' disciples marveled that he was talking with a woman (John 4:27). Jesus broke with all of that.

He spoke with a Samaritan woman at a well, a woman with a broken past whom others avoided, and revealed himself to her as the Messiah (John 4). Because of her testimony, Many Samaritans from that town believed in him (John 4:39). He allowed a sinful woman to wash his feet with her tears and declared, Your faith has saved you; go in peace (Luke 7:50). He welcomed Mary of Bethany to sit at his feet as a disciple, the place a student took before a teacher, and defended her choice: Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her (Luke 10:42). He praised a woman who anointed him and said that wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her (Mark 14:9).

Women traveled with Jesus and provided for them out of their means (Luke 8:3). When Jesus was crucified and most of the disciples had fled, There were also women looking on (Mark 15:40). And on Easter morning, the risen Christ appeared first to women and sent them to tell the apostles. Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord" (John 20:18).

Jesus did not erase the differences between men and women. He chose twelve men as apostles. But he treated women with a dignity, tenderness and respect that astonished his culture. He taught them, forgave them, healed them, received their gifts and entrusted them with the greatest news in history. Every woman who follows Christ today is following a Lord who sees her, values her and calls her to serve him.
3.theology:
Disciples, not spectators: Jesus welcomed women as learners. Mary of Bethany sat at his feet, and Martha made one of the great confessions of faith in the Gospels (John 11:27). Women are called to know Christ deeply, study his word and grow in understanding, just as men are.

Witnesses: Jesus chose women to be the first witnesses of his resurrection (Matt 28:5-8; John 20:18). In a culture that often discounted women's testimony, God gave women the privilege of announcing the central truth of the Christian faith. Every Christian woman is called to bear witness to what Christ has done.

Forgiven and restored: Many of the women who met Jesus came with painful pasts: the Samaritan woman, the sinful woman in Luke 7, Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out (Luke 8:2). Jesus did not define them by their past. He forgave, healed and restored them. No woman is beyond his grace.

The apostles and the order of the church: Jesus chose twelve men as apostles. Complementarians see this as consistent with the later New Testament pattern of male elders. Egalitarians often see it as a concession to the culture of the time. Either way, Jesus' treatment of women shows that any restriction on church office can never mean that women are less valued or less gifted.
3.examples:
The women at the cross: When the soldiers came, the disciples ran. But at the cross, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, Salome and many other women stayed (Mark 15:40-41). They could not stop the crucifixion, but they would not abandon their Lord. Faithfulness in the dark hours, simply staying when others leave, is one of the great strengths the Gospels show in women.

Supporting the mission: Luke mentions Joanna, the wife of Herod's household manager, Susanna, and many others who funded Jesus' ministry out of their own resources (Luke 8:3). Today many churches and missions are sustained by the generosity, prayers and practical care of women who rarely receive attention. Jesus notices, and Scripture records their names.

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke gives a surprising picture of Jesus' traveling ministry. Along with the twelve apostles were some women who had been healed. Their discipleship grew out of gratitude for what Jesus had done for them. And they did not merely follow. They provided for them out of their means. These women used their money and resources to support the spread of the gospel. Joanna came from Herod's court. Mary Magdalene had been set free from terrible spiritual bondage. Grace brought very different women together in the service of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching. But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, "Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me." But the Lord answered her, "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Martha was busy serving, and she was frustrated that her sister was not helping. Mary was sitting at the Lord's feet, the position of a disciple learning from a teacher. Jesus did not condemn Martha's service, but he gently corrected her anxious heart: Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. And he honored Mary's choice to learn. Women are not only called to serve Christ with their hands. They are invited to sit at his feet, to learn his word and to know him.

verseByVerse.quote: Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman's testimony, "He told me all that I ever did." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A woman who had been married five times and was living with a man who was not her husband became one of the first evangelists in the Gospels. She went back to the town that probably looked down on her and said, in effect, "Come and see a man who told me everything I ever did." Her testimony was simple and honest, and Many Samaritans from that town believed in him. God delights to use unlikely people, including women with painful pasts, to point others to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord"—and that he had said these things to her. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The first person to see the risen Jesus, according to John, was Mary Magdalene. She came to the tomb weeping, and Jesus called her by name. Then he sent her with a message to the disciples. She became the first to announce, I have seen the Lord. The central claim of Christianity, that Jesus is alive, was first spoken by a woman. Every Christian woman who tells others about Jesus is following in Mary's footsteps.

3.reflection:
Which of the women Jesus met do you relate to most, and why?

Mary sat at Jesus' feet while Martha served. Where does your life need more of Mary, and where does it need more of Martha?

What does the choice of women as the first witnesses of the resurrection teach us about how God values women?

How could you use your resources, like the women in Luke 8, to support the work of the gospel?

4.title: Wives: Strength Under Christ
4.overview:
Few Bible verses are more misunderstood today than this one: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord (Eph 5:22). To many modern ears, submission sounds like weakness, inferiority or even abuse. But when we read what Scripture actually says, we find something very different.

First, this instruction is addressed to wives, not to women in general. Paul says your own husbands. Women are not called to submit to all men. Second, it is voluntary. Paul speaks to the wife herself, not to the husband. Nowhere does the Bible tell husbands to make their wives submit. Third, it is as to the Lord. A wife's submission is ultimately an act of trust in Christ, not in her husband's perfection. Fourth, it has limits. No wife is called to follow her husband into sin, for We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and no wife is called to submit to abuse.

Submission in marriage means that a wife honors her husband's God-given responsibility to lead, supports him, respects him (Eph 5:33) and seeks to help him lead well. It does not mean silence. A wise wife speaks, advises, disagrees when necessary and brings all her gifts to the marriage. The woman of Proverbs 31 buys fields, runs a business, helps the poor and speaks with wisdom, and The heart of her husband trusts in her (Prov 31:11).

Christians differ on how to understand these passages. Complementarians, whose view these studies follow, see a real and loving pattern of headship and submission in marriage, rooted in creation and modeled on Christ and the church. Egalitarians often stress Ephesians 5:21, submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ, and see the specific instructions to wives as applying Christian humility within first-century household customs. Both agree that husbands and wives are equal before God, that the husband must love sacrificially, and that no one may use these verses to oppress.
4.theology:
Submission is not inferiority: The head of Christ is God (1 Cor 11:3), and the Son willingly submits to the Father (1 Cor 15:28), though he is fully equal to him. Submission within an order of roles says nothing about lesser worth. A wife who submits to her husband is doing something Christ himself does.

The church and Christ: Paul grounds his instruction in a greater reality: as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands (Eph 5:24). Christian marriage is a living picture of the gospel. The husband's sacrificial love pictures Christ's love, and the wife's glad trust and respect pictures the church's response to Christ.

The limits of submission: In everything (Eph 5:24) does not include sin. The same Bible that calls wives to submit calls every believer to obey God first. Scripture shows godly women who wisely resisted sinful men. Submission never requires a wife to endure abuse, cover up crime or disobey God.

Beauty of the heart: Peter urges wives to cultivate the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious (1 Pet 3:4). A gentle and quiet spirit is not a matter of personality. Outgoing, energetic women can have it. It is a heart at rest in God, not anxious, controlling or fearful. Peter adds that such women do not fear anything that is frightening (1 Pet 3:6).
4.examples:
Abigail: wisdom in a hard marriage: Abigail was married to Nabal, a man described as harsh and badly behaved (1 Sam 25:3). When his foolishness put the whole household in danger, Abigail acted quickly, met David and persuaded him not to take revenge. David said, Blessed be your discretion (1 Sam 25:33). Abigail shows that godly womanhood includes courage, initiative and wisdom, especially when a husband is failing.

Winning without a word: Many Christian women are married to men who do not share their faith, or whose faith has grown cold. Peter gives them hope: husbands may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives (1 Pet 3:1). This does not forbid speaking about Christ. It means that constant pressure and nagging rarely win hearts, while a life of respect, purity and peace speaks powerfully over time.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Notice the words as to the Lord. A wife submits to her husband as an expression of her devotion to Christ. Her husband may be imperfect, but her obedience is directed to the perfect Lord. Paul then explains the pattern: the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church. And he immediately adds that Christ is its Savior. The headship Paul describes is the headship of a Savior who dies for his bride. Paul then spends far more words calling husbands to that kind of love (Eph 5:25-33). A wife is not called to submit to a tyrant, but to trust a husband who is himself commanded to love her like Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter writes to wives whose husbands do not obey the word, women married to unbelievers. In a world where wives were expected to follow their husbands' religion, these women had chosen Christ. Peter does not tell them to leave their husbands or to argue them into faith. He tells them to live in such a way that their husbands may be won without a word, through their respectful and pure conduct. A wife's godly life can be one of the most powerful sermons a husband ever hears.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter is not forbidding women to care about their appearance, wear jewelry or do their hair. He is saying where true beauty lies. External beauty fades, and our culture's obsession with it leaves many women anxious and insecure. But the hidden person of the heart has an imperishable beauty. A gentle and quiet spirit is precious in God's sight. Other people may overlook it. God never does. This is beauty that grows with age rather than fading.

verseByVerse.quote: An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels. The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain. She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The ESV notes that Proverbs 31:10-31 is an acrostic poem, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It is an A-to-Z portrait of a wise, godly woman, not a checklist every woman must complete. She is far more precious than jewels. Her husband trusts her completely. She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life. And the poem goes on to show her strength: she buys a field, plants a vineyard, runs a business, cares for the poor and speaks with wisdom. The ESV notes that verse 17, She dresses herself with strength, is literally "She girds her loins", a picture of preparing for hard work. Biblical womanhood is not passive. It is strong.

4.reflection:
What misunderstandings of the word "submission" have you heard? How does Ephesians 5 correct them?

Why is it important that the call to submit is addressed to wives themselves, and that it has limits?

Abigail acted wisely when her husband was foolish. What does her story teach about the strength and initiative of a godly wife?

What does "a gentle and quiet spirit" look like in a woman with a strong, outgoing personality?

5.title: Women in the Church: Gifts, Ministry and Order
5.overview:
The New Testament church was full of women serving Christ. Women prayed and prophesied in the gatherings (1 Cor 11:5; Acts 21:9), just as Joel had promised that your sons and your daughters shall prophesy (Acts 2:17). Older women taught and trained younger women (Titus 2:3-5). Priscilla, together with her husband Aquila, took the gifted preacher Apollos aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26). Phoebe was a servant of the church at Cenchreae and a generous patron, and Paul probably entrusted her with carrying his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:1-2). Lydia opened her home to Paul and to the believers in Philippi (Acts 16:15, 40). Euodia and Syntyche labored side by side with Paul in the gospel (Phil 4:3).

At the same time, Paul writes, Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet. For Adam was formed first, then Eve (1 Tim 2:11-13). How do these fit together?

Complementarians, whose view these studies follow, understand Paul to be reserving the office of elder or pastor, and the authoritative teaching of the whole church that belongs to it, to qualified men. They note that Paul grounds this in creation, not culture. Women may and should use their gifts in countless other ways: teaching women and children, prophesying, evangelizing, counseling, leading ministries, serving as deacons in many churches, showing hospitality and mercy, and much more.

Egalitarians read the same passages differently. Many believe Paul was addressing a specific problem in Ephesus, such as false teachers influencing untaught women, and they point to Deborah the judge (Judg 4:4), to Phoebe, and to Junia, whom Paul describes as well known to the apostles (Rom 16:7), as evidence that women may hold any office. Faithful Christians who love Scripture hold both views. What both should agree on is that the church is poorer whenever women's gifts are neglected.
5.theology:
Every believer gifted: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good (1 Cor 12:7). As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another (1 Pet 4:10). The Holy Spirit gives gifts to women as freely as to men, and the church needs every one of them.

Women are to learn: Before Paul says anything else in 1 Timothy 2:11, he says, Let a woman learn. In a culture where women were often denied religious education, this was a remarkable command. Christian women are to study God's word deeply.

Office and gifts: Complementarians distinguish between the office of elder, the overseer responsible for teaching and governing the whole church, and the many gifts and ministries open to all. They also note the ESV's footnotes that Phoebe may be called a "deaconess" (Rom 16:1) and that Junia may be read "Junias", with the apostles possibly meaning "messengers" (Rom 16:7). The Reformed tradition has differed on whether women may serve as deacons, but has generally held that the elder's office is for men.

Spiritual mothers: Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior... They are to teach what is good, and so train the young women (Titus 2:3-4). Some of the most powerful ministry in any church is done by older women who disciple younger women in faith, marriage, motherhood and the daily Christian life.
5.examples:
More than the kitchen and the nursery: Some churches have limited women's service to cooking, cleaning and childcare. Those are valuable ministries, and Jesus honors them. But the New Testament shows women teaching, evangelizing, supporting missions, opening their homes for churches, prophesying and laboring in the gospel. A church that holds complementarian convictions should be the first to open every door of service that Scripture leaves open.

A spiritual mother: Paul greets Rufus also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well (Rom 16:13). We know nothing else about her, except that she cared for the great apostle like a son. Many women without children of their own, or whose children are grown, become spiritual mothers to younger believers. That is ministry of the highest value.

verseByVerse.quote: Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good, and so train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul gives older women a teaching ministry. They are to be reverent in behavior, self-controlled in speech and habits, and then teach what is good. Their students are the younger women, and the curriculum is the whole Christian life: loving husbands and children, self-control, purity, managing the home, kindness and a godly marriage. Notice the reason: that the word of God may not be reviled. When Christian women live and teach well, the gospel is honored. Younger women need older women, and older women need to see that their experience is a gift for the church.

verseByVerse.quote: He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Apollos was eloquent and knew the Scriptures well, but his understanding was incomplete. Priscilla and Aquila heard him, took him aside privately and explained the gospel more accurately. Notice that Priscilla's name comes first, as it often does in the New Testament, which may suggest that she was especially prominent. Here a woman, together with her husband, taught a gifted male preacher in a private setting. Complementarians see this as fully consistent with Paul's teaching, since it was not the public teaching office of the church. Egalitarians see it as evidence of women teaching men more broadly. Either way, Priscilla's knowledge of Scripture strengthened the church.

verseByVerse.quote: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Phoebe is the first person Paul greets in Romans, and he commends her warmly. She is a servant of the church at Cenchreae, and the ESV notes that servant may be translated "deaconess". She was also a patron of many and of myself as well, a woman who used her resources to support the church and its ministers. Many believe she carried this very letter to Rome. The most important letter Paul ever wrote may have been placed in the hands of a woman to deliver and perhaps to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet. For Adam was formed first, then Eve; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This passage begins with a command that was radical in its day: Let a woman learn. Then Paul adds a limit: I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man. Complementarians understand this to refer to the office and authority of elders in the gathered church, and they note that Paul's reason is creation: For Adam was formed first, then Eve. Egalitarians often read it as a temporary instruction for a church troubled by false teaching. This is a matter on which believers who love the Bible disagree, and it should be discussed with humility and charity. For every woman, the passage begins with an invitation: learn God's word, deeply and gladly.

5.reflection:
Make a list of all the ways women served in the New Testament church. Which of these are encouraged in your church today?

How would you explain the complementarian and egalitarian readings of 1 Timothy 2:11-13 fairly to someone who disagreed with you?

Titus 2 calls older women to train younger women. Who has been a spiritual mother to you, or whom could you encourage?

What gifts has God given you, and how are you using them to serve his church?

6.title: Beauty That Lasts: Singleness, Motherhood and the Fear of the LORD
6.overview:
The Proverbs 31 poem ends with the key to everything: Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised (Prov 31:30). Charm can deceive. Physical beauty fades. What lasts is a heart that reverences and trusts God.

That truth frees women in every season of life. Many women feel pressure to find their identity in marriage or in motherhood. But Scripture honors women in every circumstance. Paul says that the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit (1 Cor 7:34). Singleness can be a season, or a lifetime, of devoted service to Christ. Anna, widowed after only seven years of marriage, spent decades in the temple worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day, and she was one of the first to recognize the baby Jesus as the Redeemer (Luke 2:37-38).

Motherhood is a high calling. Children are a heritage from the LORD (Ps 127:3). Hannah prayed through years of childlessness, then gave her son Samuel back to God: For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition (1 Sam 1:27). Timothy's sincere faith dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice (2 Tim 1:5). Generations of believers owe their faith to praying mothers and grandmothers.

And Scripture speaks tenderly to women who long for children and have none. He gives the barren woman a home, making her the joyous mother of children (Ps 113:9). Sometimes God answers that prayer with children of her own. Sometimes he gives spiritual children through her love and ministry. Either way, her worth before God is complete in Christ.

Finally, every Christian woman looks forward to a day when all fading beauty will be replaced by glory. The whole church is Christ's bride, and at the end of history the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready (Rev 19:7). That is the destiny of every woman who belongs to him.
6.theology:
The fear of the LORD: The whole book of Proverbs begins and ends with the fear of the LORD. The excellent woman is not praised first for her productivity or her beauty but for her reverent trust in God. This is the root from which all her other virtues grow.

Singleness as a gift: Paul, himself single, says each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another (1 Cor 7:7). A single woman is not an incomplete woman. Jesus, the most fully human person who ever lived, was single. The church should honor single women and give them a full place in its family life.

Motherhood and spiritual motherhood: Mothers shape generations (2 Tim 1:5), and Titus 2 calls young women to love their children. But motherhood in the church is wider than biology. Every mature woman can nurture faith in others, as Rufus's mother did for Paul (Rom 16:13).

Hope for every season: The capable woman of Proverbs 31 laughs at the time to come (Prov 31:25). She can face aging, loss and the unknown future without fear, because her hope is in God. For the Christian woman, that hope is sure: she belongs to Christ, and her imperishable beauty will be revealed in glory.
6.examples:
Anna in the temple: Anna had every reason to be bitter. Her husband died after seven years, and she lived as a widow into her eighties. Instead, she gave herself to worship and prayer. And God rewarded her faithfulness by letting her see the Messiah and tell others about him (Luke 2:36-38). A life that looks small to the world can be rich and fruitful before God.

Hannah's prayer: Hannah was mocked for her childlessness and misunderstood even by the priest. She took her grief to God and poured out her soul. When God gave her Samuel, she did not cling to him but dedicated him to the LORD. Her story comforts women who wait, and it challenges mothers to hold their children with open hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the climax of the Proverbs 31 poem. Charm can be a mask. Beauty is vain, fleeting like a breath. Our culture spends enormous energy on both. But the praise goes to a woman who fears the LORD. To fear the LORD is to live in reverent awe of him, trusting and obeying him. Every woman can have that beauty, whatever her appearance, age or circumstances. And unlike charm and outward beauty, it grows richer with the years.

verseByVerse.quote: and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul is not saying that married women do not care about the Lord, or that marriage is spiritually second-class. He is describing a practical reality. Marriage rightly brings responsibilities: a wife cares about how to please her husband. A single woman has a unique freedom to give undivided attention to the things of the Lord. Paul saw singleness as an opportunity, not a tragedy. Single women in the church are not waiting for their lives to begin. They can serve Christ now with a devotion that married women often cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him. Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD." And he worshiped the LORD there. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Hannah had begged God for a child through years of tears. When her prayer was answered, she kept her promise and brought young Samuel to serve at the house of the LORD. Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. Every Christian mother must learn this lesson. Our children are gifts from God, not possessions. We raise them for him, and we release them into his hands. Samuel became one of Israel's greatest prophets, and it began with a praying mother.

verseByVerse.quote: I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul traces Timothy's faith back two generations: first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice. Timothy's father was a Greek (Acts 16:1), and there is no sign that he shared their faith. These two women taught Timothy the Scriptures from childhood (2 Tim 3:15). A grandmother's prayers and a mother's teaching shaped a pastor who would lead churches and receive two letters of Scripture. Many women do their most lasting work at a kitchen table with an open Bible and a child beside them.

6.reflection:
Proverbs 31:30 says a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised. How is the fear of the LORD different from being charming or beautiful?

How can your church honor and include single women more fully in its life and ministry?

What did Hannah's example of "lending" Samuel to the LORD teach you about holding children, or other gifts, with open hands?

Who were the "Lois and Eunice" figures in your own faith? How might you pass faith on to the next generation?
